slides.title: Real-World Coordinate-Plane Problems; Perimeter
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: every side of a figure on the grid, and the two ways across a map.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is today's idea with only straight sides: a perimeter adds every side — 7, 3, 7 and 3, across zero for both. Today some sides are slanted. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the rule and the example.
slides.note:
(3, 2), (6, 2) and (6, 6): two sides lie on grid lines, 3 across and 4 up; the third is slanted, and the other two are its legs: 9 + 16 = 25, 5. The perimeter adds all three: 12 units. Counting the squares a slanted side crosses does not measure it (board 9).
OFF: 'Every side counts. A slanted side gets its triangle.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
On a map whose streets are the grid lines, the walk from A to B goes 6 blocks across and 8 up — 14 blocks — and the straight line (a bird, a zip line, a tunnel) is the hypotenuse, 10. The straight path is 4 blocks shorter; it is shorter whenever the points share neither an x nor a y.
OFF: 'The streets add the legs. The straight line is the hypotenuse.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
This triangle has no square corner, but its height — from the top corner straight down to the base — makes two, each with legs 3 and 5: each slanted side is √34. Keep the root (or the calculator's whole value) to the last step: 6 + 5.831 + 5.831 = 17.662, so 17.7. Rounding each side first gives 6 + 5.8 + 5.8 = 17.6 — a different answer.
OFF: 'No square corner? Make two. Round once, at the end.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which sides lie on grid lines before anyone measures: DE and EF. DF is slanted — it gets its own triangle, and DE and EF are its legs.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: DE: 3 − (−3) = 6; EF: 6 − (−2) = 8; DF: 36 + 64 = 100, 10. P = 24 units. A board with 14 left DF out; one with 28 took DF as 6 + 8.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Across 4 − (−5) = 9 and up 5 − (−7) = 12, so the slanted side is √225 = 15 and P = 9 + 12 + 15 = 36 — a board with 21 left the slanted side out.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A map: the streets and the straight line.
slides.note: Ask what 'along the streets' means on this map: on the grid lines — across, then up. The straight line is the slanted segment.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Across 4 − (−3) = 7, up 3 − (−2) = 5. The streets add them: 12 blocks. The straight line: 49 + 25 = 74, √74 ≈ 8.60, so 8.6 blocks — 3.4 blocks shorter. A board with 12 for both answered the streets twice.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Across −2 − (−5) = 3 and down 4 − (−4) = 8: by the streets 11 blocks, straight √73 ≈ 8.54, so 8.5 — a board with 11 for the straight line added the legs.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: AB = 12 across zero, BC = 5, AC: 144 + 25 = 169, 13. P = 30. A board with 17 left AC out; one with 34 took AC as 12 + 5.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: 4 and 9 on grid lines; the slanted side √97 ≈ 9.849. P ≈ 22.849, so 22.8 — one rounding, at the end.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The height from C lands at (1, −6) and splits the base 5 and 9 — not in half. AC: 25 + 144 = 169, 13; BC: 81 + 144 = 225, 15. P = 14 + 13 + 15 = 42. A board with 40 took both slanted sides as 13.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option A left the slanted side out, option B added the legs for it, option C forgot the square root. Split (no option near two-thirds)? Sixty seconds, convince your neighbour, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Across 12, up 5: the streets are 17 blocks, the straight line 13 — 4 blocks shorter. A board with 13 or 17 answered one path; the question asks the difference.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option B added two sides, option C gave the perimeter, option D read one corner's coordinates as the legs (and 6-8-10 is a triple, so it looks right). Split? Sixty seconds, convince your neighbour, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Across 9, down 5 — both across zero. 81 + 25 = 106, √106 ≈ 10.30, so 10.3 m.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the trailhead is bait. Camp to lake: across 5, up 12, 169, 13 miles.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: the error named and the length found.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.

slides.note: IXL: every listed skill is required, SmartScore 67. Due at the start of the next class.
